summary:

The post Britain’s education system has a data problem appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Rob Phillpotts, Chief data officer at Jisc.

Ministers want colleges and universities to become more responsive to skills shortages, local economies and changing labour markets. The information infrastructure on which those ambitions depend is not yet up to the job.

Everyday services have reshaped what we expect from data. We assume information will be available quickly, services will respond to needs, and decisions will reflect what is happening now, not months ago. Algorithms raise questions about transparency and trust, but fast, reliable and usable data is now part of how modern services are delivered.

The same expectation applies to tertiary education, which is central to the government’s ambitions for growth, productivity, social mobility, lifelong learning and regional innovation. Providers need to understand demand, make timely recruitment decisions and help learners move between college, university and employment. Students expect institutions to respond to their needs at pace, so providers must be able to mobilise information quickly.

However, the education system has a data problem. The data infrastructure supporting this is not equipped to meet these ambitions. Providers supply similar information, in different formats, to different organisations. Across the sector, legacy systems and under-investment have left many without the data capability needed. System-wide insight is hard to achieve because data does not link or respond quickly enough to emerging needs (although the in-year programme aims to improve timeliness of HE data).

The problem is pressing

The challenge has several ingredients. First, no single authority is responsible for coordinating data across the system. Platforms are not always interoperable, data sources do not link sufficiently and learner identity is not applied consistently.

Second, the landscape is becoming more complex. Education policy rightly varies across the four UK nations, and various government and statutory bodies hold distinct responsibilities from further education through to higher education and research. Devolving more to the regions could make the data landscape harder still to navigate.

Third, persistent financial pressure means providers must reduce avoidable costs while making better decisions. Data should be a real enabler, not just a way of understanding the student body: student support should be portable, learner records should link skills and credits across the system, and careers services should draw on a connected understanding of future regional demand, not just what previous graduates did.

Change is needed if individual institutions and the sector are to resolve these challenges and unlock the potential of a data-enriched sector.

What value could be unlocked?

There are already areas where better data coordination would make a difference:

Institutions could spend less time resubmitting similar data for different purposes, and statutory bodies could reduce the cost of processing fragmented data.

Better understanding of graduate outcomes, and so of the value of education to graduates’ lives, wellbeing and contribution to society, requires agreement across multiple bodies.

Shared ownership of cross-system data is needed for topics such as higher education delivered in colleges, university estates, climate data, and definitions like ‘degree apprenticeship’, ‘estranged student’ or ‘care leaver’.

Emerging priorities, including regional innovation and skills, need coordinated, consistent and comparable data arrangements.

Learner progress through the system and between providers could be facilitated, tracked and potentially transformed with a common learner identity.

Whole system issue

The tertiary data system is complex, and this is a long-term, multi-faceted issue. Jisc, as the designated data body (DDB) in England, has a key role in HE, but the system includes many organisations, including UCAS, SLC, OfS, DfE, Medr, SfC and other government departments and statutory bodies. Jisc already works with many of these to bring people together, coordinate approaches and deliver services. However, progress depends heavily on individual relationships, bilateral engagement and programme-specific collaboration.

In England, for example, the Office for Students determines what data the DDB can collect and publish for HE regulatory purposes, and Jisc fulfils this within a framework. That framework remains important, but the next stage of reform and ambition may require a more joined-up, system-wide tertiary level mechanism for decision-making.

A way forward

Resolving these challenges will be a large-scale undertaking and cannot happen all at once, but practical, no-regret measures could improve the rate of progress and further develop our understanding of the challenges ahead. A first step could be to enhance governance for tertiary data, bringing together the principal data and statutory bodies, the devolved governments and the sector: DfE, OfS, UCAS, Jisc, UKRI, Medr and SLC, alongside organisations such as UUK, AoC, GuildHE and IHE.

However, our long-term ambition must extend beyond coordinating data silos and convening to collaborate, to a joined-up approach that resolves cross-system issues and puts learners at the centre in the long term. If a stronger foundation is needed, government may need to consider legislative change.

Any reform should respect how education is delivered in each nation and underpin the functions statutory bodies must perform. The goal should be high-quality data at the heart of evolving education services, and a foundation for a more coherent, efficient and future-ready tertiary system.

title: Neet ideas: what’s in Alan Milburn’s report on young people not in education, employment or training?
summary:
Former minister’s 278-page report calls for changes to employment regulations, education, healthcare and benefits

  • Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts

  • Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people

Five months on from a first report detailing the growing crisis of young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet), Alan Milburn has produced his recommendations on how to tackle it. Set out over 278 pages, they amount to, as he readily accepts, a major rethink of everything from employment regulations to education, healthcare and benefits.

Here is what he has said.

Continue reading...
full_text:
1. The context

While this was in part covered by the first report, Milburn is at pains to begin the new volume with his belief that the issue of Neets is not a failure of the younger generation but a case of them being let down by a series of structural factors. “The young people I have met over the last year are not asking for an easier life. They are asking for a fair chance to build one,” he writes.

The answer must be radical, he says. “This cannot be fixed by tweaking the edges of the existing system. The response now has to be full throttle: not another initiative or another round of incremental reform, but transformational change.”

At the centre of the proposed new system is a youth opportunity service (YOS), which would offer young people support in areas such as training and health – and would in return expect participation.

2. The goals

Currently, about 13.5% of people aged 16-24 in the UK are classified as Neet, the highest proportion in Europe outside Romania. This is not a new problem, the report notes, pointing out that the Neet rate has stayed above 10% for most of the past 25 years.

The aim over a decade-long transformational plan would be to match the records of the best-performing European nations on this metric, such as the Netherlands and Denmark. While Milburn talks playfully of aiming for “Neet zero”, he says this means an eventual consistent rate of about 5%.

He says the policies in his plan would get the Neet rate to about 6.8% by 2036.

3. Employers and the labour market

Noting that youth employment has declined even as overall employment rose, Milburn says opportunities are limited by issues affecting young people – for example, a lack of connections to secure work experience or first jobs – and also employers, including the costs of taking on staff and regulatory complexities.

The report says this is worsened by a lack of government help. While Denmark spends about 1% of GDP on all-age hiring incentives and subsidies, in the UK it is about 0.1%.

The report sets out a series of recommendations, including:

Doubling the salary threshold for employer national insurance for entry-level jobs for young people in retail and hospitality, possibly then expanded to other sectors.

Extending the existing youth jobs grant, which gives up to £3,000 to employers who takes on a staff member on universal credit for at least six months, so it also applies to people not on benefits, with extra incentives for small employers and people facing barriers, such as those with disabilities or care leavers.

Avoid minimum pay rates being a barrier – for example, any moves to put young people’s minimum wages closer the adult rate should be judged “against the critical goal of protecting youth employment”.

This should be matched with increased simplicity for companies, with a single digital gateway leading to all the schemes set up to help young workers, and more clarity on help for workers with disabilities.

All this would be united in a so-called youth opportunity test, under which any future tax or regulatory policy changes would look at their effect on young workers, set out in a law.

4. Education and training

The report notes that this is a long-term issue, with many of the indicators of future Neet status, such as low attainment and poor attendance, being clear during childhood. Milburn also says that while countries with low Neet rates take vocational skills seriously, in England “technical education has too often been regarded as for somebody else’s child”.

Among changes the report recommends are:

More investment in early years provision, such as family hubs, and individual support in school if a student is seen as being at “material risk of disengagement”.

Less use of school exclusion where possible. The report notes that the Netherlands has a permanent exclusion rate 73% lower than England’s.

More focus in school on preparedness for work, as well as passing exams.

More investment in further education and in apprenticeships, with greater financial incentives for employers who hire apprentices.

University courses “must be able to demonstrate clear value for learners, employers and the wider economy,” with funding withdrawn for poorly performing examples.

5. Health

The report identifies health as central to the Neets issue, with more than half of young people in this position reporting a health condition.

Milburn says much of this is down to a health service “designed to diagnose and treat illness” rather than intervening earlier, and that is not aimed at helping people into work, with diagnoses and the fit note system creating a “binary” mindset.

It recommends:

Much quicker access to health and mental health assistance, long before a formal diagnosis, based around the new YOS system. If someone has a health issue, their YOS-designated adviser can point them towards advice and help, potentially including talking therapies.

A move away from GPs issuing fit notes, which would instead become the responsibility of other health experts such as occupational therapists or non-clinicians such as employment advisers.

6. Social security

The report is highly critical of what it calls a current system that can trap people in dependence. “It asks a young person what they cannot do before it asks them what, with the right support, they could. The welfare system for too many young people has become a trap when it ought to be a springboard.”

At the same time, it argues that crudely cutting rates or entitlement do not work, “fiscally nor morally”. It says: “If they leave young people destitute, then costs merely show up somewhere else on the state’s balance sheet in health, housing or criminal justice. Spending less is not the same as succeeding. The test is whether lives and trajectories change.”

Saying more must be invested in helping people on benefits, it recommends:

A new “opportunity guarantee” for a place in education, training or work for anyone aged 18 to 24, along with a “support guarantee” for the support required for them to do this. Based on significant investment, these must be in place before the changes begin, the report says.

Among the options under the guarantee are: a government-subsidised job with employers receiving £3,000 for each young person they recruit – more for smaller businesses or when the employee has extra needs; an FE place, or technical or university learning as appropriate; an apprenticeship; a work placement of up to 12 weeks; structured volunteering such as conservation, community gardening or a cadetship; help to create a business.

The “backstop” to all this would be a state-financed six-month job with an employer.

The creation of a new “youth allowance”, set at the under-25 rate of universal credit.

A new “health and disability fund” operated by the local YOS to help with extra costs, which are or might be time-limited.

An “additional cost allowance”, replacing personal independence payment for young people, when their disability-related extra costs “are significant, established and ongoing”. The report says eligibility “would be more closely targeted at those with demonstrable extra costs for functional needs that are long-term and enduring”, with an aim of enabling independence and participation.

A “severe and complex needs insurance”, a more generous long-term award without a qualifying period, for those with the most profound disabilities, and where it is clear they are unlikely ever to be able to work.

With this would come changes to “actively reward and enable participation”, for example allowing young people to keep more earnings before benefits are cut, and extra money for people who undertake civic service.

With this would come a responsibility to engage. Someone who persistently refuses to do so would lose their youth allowance benefit, but only after “multiple attempts to re-engage and understand what has gone wrong”.

7. The costs

While much of the media buildup to the report has been questions about whether the changes could result in benefits payments overall starting to fall in this parliament, Milburn makes it plain that this must be a longer-term process, with investment preceding savings.

The report says: “While the intention is to hit the ground running, the speed of change has to be sustained over time. This is a 10-year plan, not a one-year sprint … Short-termism has been a constant feature of our country’s approach to this issue over the last 50 years.”

This would involve an initial investment of £500m in 2027-28, taken from existing spending, which would then “ramp up”.

By 2036-37, the report says, annual investment would be about £5.8bn, covering the guarantees, hiring incentives and health, education and skills changes, offset by £3.6bn of savings and £2.4bn in increased tax revenues, covering lower welfare payments and more tax receipts.

title: Childhood neglect, unmet needs, mental health struggles: this is the making of a Neet | Mark Mon-Williams
summary:

  • Mark Mon-Williams is chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Leeds and professor of psychology at Bradford Institute of Health Research

full_text:
Alan Milburn and Peter Fonagy have, between them, expertly diagnosed the UK’s illness. Their reviews show we don’t just have a Neet crisis. Or a school absence crisis. Or a Send crisis. We have a neglected childhood crisis that will wreck the country’s long-term prosperity if we just keep patching over these symptoms.

The solution to any problem starts with understanding its causes, and Milburn and Fonagy provide a thoughtful analysis. I have worked closely with both of them, being a topic group member for Fonagy’s independent review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism, and supporting Milburn with data analytics. Their reviews have followed the evidence, all of which shows a system neglecting children at scale. We have decreased benefits and slashed the support provided to children: today4.5 million children are living in poverty. When these children grow up and are diagnosed with anxiety and depression, impeding their ability to work, they are often castigated as feckless snowflakes. It is easier to do this than admit that we have failed a generation, and that this is the predictable consequence of political decisions.

Born in Bradford, our longitudinal birth cohort programme launched in 2007 to follow the development of 13,500 children and their families, has been tracking these changes in real time, and our Child of the North consortium has synthesised the national evidence. Our findings show how childhood disadvantage accumulates into young adulthood. The science is extensive and methodologically complex, but the findings can be readily grasped through the life of an archetypal child who we will call Tracey.

Tracey is a young person desperate for education, employment or training. Like many others, she has special educational needs, anxiety and depression. We might think Tracey is Neet because she lives in a rundown area without transport links to education, employment, or training. But most young people in Bradford lack good transport, so this is only part of the story.

This is where our connected datasets are so powerful, as they allow us to travel back in time and piece together Tracey’s life from birth. Tracey’s mum was anxious and depressed and living in poverty when she was pregnant. These risk factors are known to hinder children’s development, but the signal was ignored. In fact, Tracey’s mum got less support than her middle-class peers because she couldn’t get to an antenatal group, while health visitor support was being slashed for expectant mums.

Tracey was born prematurely with health complications. Fortunately, our brilliant NHS ensured that her medical needs were met. Unfortunately, information about Tracey wasn’t shared with the other public services that would deal with the consequences of her early health problems downstream. The NHS also couldn’t address the impoverished environment in which Tracey spent her early years.

It turns out that brain science can be surprisingly easy to understand. Children need healthy environments for healthy brain growth. If children grow up in impoverished environments, they won’t develop the core skills needed to achieve and thrive in education. This means they will, by definition, have educational needs that go beyond the pedagogical support required by children whose families can access developmentally supportive environments.

The impoverished preschool environment means that Tracey starts school without the core skills needed to thrive. This is not a surprise to our Bradford researchers, who can see her history of risk factors. But it is a surprise for her teachers, who did not receive any of this information from Tracey’s mum or other public services.

Tracey struggles in primary school and her needs are not well supported: her mum cannot navigate the complex processes needed to secure the clinical diagnosis that would trigger support for her neurodevelopmental and educational needs.

It should be no surprise that Tracey struggles when she arrives at secondary school. But it is a surprise to the secondary school, because it wasn’t provided with the recorded information that screams Tracey needs love, understanding and help.

Tracey doesn’t feel included at secondary school or that she belongs there. Once more, brain science can be surprisingly easy to understand. The brain generates feelings of anxiety when faced with environments that feel hostile, and feelings of depression when hope is eroded.

Tracey attends a school with an outstanding Ofsted rating, but her own results are not helping its league table position. The school gently encourages her away from class and Tracey starts to miss school on an increasingly frequent basis. Before Tracey can sit her GCSEs, the school suggests that perhaps she should find another school or be educated at home. This is an unscrupulous yet perfectly rational response within an education system that rewards attainment over inclusion. Unfortunately, the science shows an unequivocal relationship between school absence and becoming Neet, so there is no surprise when Tracey ends up not in education, employment or training.

This all appears inevitable when viewed in hindsight. But it isn’t. Patterns in data are not fixed outcomes. We know that schemes like Sure Start in England, mercilessly cut by the coalition government, can transform children’s lives and help them enjoy healthy, productive futures. Our Bradford research shows an earlier diagnosis of neurodevelopmental issues is associated with lower risk of teenage mental health problems, and that “inclusive” schools show lower Neet rates. Early risk factors are signals for intervention, not fatalistic trapdoors. Young people don’t become Neet overnight, and every day offers an opportunity to either reduce childhood risks or let them accumulate.

Why Tracey? Our hypothetical child is homage to Tracey Emin. Her work Why I Never Became a Dancer uses art to capture these scientific truths and shows how one child overcame childhood trauma to become a world-leading artist.

Compassion shines from the Milburn and Fonagy reviews. We must share their compassion. Our children need love, understanding and a national commitment to overcome the UK’s neglected childhood crisis.

Tracey’s story is not only about poverty or adversity but also about system failure. The social safety net is cut without consideration of the long-term consequences. Health services treat medical problems, but cannot see or address living conditions. Information isn’t shared between services. Schools are rewarded for exam results, rather than helping children. Support, rationed by thresholds, only arrives at crisis points.

The answer cannot be another sticking plaster for young people transitioning into adulthood. We need to reimagine how we support children from birth so our young people and economy can thrive. This means reshaping the public sector around improving children’s lives, while tackling the deprivation that creates adversity in the first place.

Andy Burnham is right when he says that this demands a generational response. We must all get behind a national commitment to transform childhood, recognising that the anxiety, depression and lost opportunities experienced by too many young people are not inevitable. They are the consequences of choices we have made as a society, and choices we have the power to change.

title: As AI Changes How Students Approach College, Old Challenges Persist
summary:
As AI Changes How Students Approach College, Old Challenges Persist colleen.flaherty Tue, 11/17/2026 - 03:00 AM The student experience is in transition, but unmet financial needs and mental health continue to limit students’ success, according to new Student Voice data. Byline(s) Colleen Flaherty As AI Changes How Students Approach College, Old Challenges Persist
colleen.flaherty Tue, 11/17/2026 - 03:00 AM

The student experience is in transition, but unmet financial needs and mental health continue to limit students’ success, according to new Student Voice data.

Byline(s)
Colleen Flaherty
full_text:
Students’ assessment of their educational quality remains high. And while artificial intelligence is introducing new anxieties—and its implementation thus far leaves something to be desired—it’s also empowering some students. Still, out-of-the-classroom issues continue to bear on students’ academic success, according to data from Inside Higher Ed’s main Student Voice survey of 2026–27. The sample includes 5,034 undergraduates from 310 mostly public two- and four-year institutions.

Among the survey’s top-line findings:

About a third of students each say generative or agentic AI helps them complete coursework and study more efficiently (34 percent) and feel more confident understanding and taking on difficult concepts (33 percent). But a quarter say they have changed how they write to avoid being falsely flagged by AI detectors.

Students’ top priorities for responsible AI use in higher education are to help them learn, not just do the work for them (65 percent) and to be transparent about when and how AI is being used (60 percent).

More than eight in 10 students (81 percent) rate the quality of their education as good or excellent, but just 24 percent are highly confident in their institution’s efforts to keep that education affordable.

Mental health is the most commonly cited barrier to academic success and persistence, cited by 41 percent of students. Financial pressure is a close second, at 37 percent. Six in 10 students (61 percent) have also gone without at least one essential—such as food, housing or transportation—in the last year for financial reasons.

Nearly a third of students (32 percent) haven’t participated in any extra- or co-curricular activities since they enrolled, jumping to 66 percent of community college students. Both two- and four-year students are most likely to agree that introducing financial incentives would boost their participation.

More than half of students (54 percent) want their institution to prioritize job pipelines and internships to better prepare them for the labor market. And while most are stressed about some aspect of preparing for life after college, 80 percent somewhat or strongly agree they’re being well prepared to succeed in today’s job market.

While few students report clear insight into their program’s postgraduate outcomes (17 percent), most value college beyond postgraduate earnings—and personal interest or passion in the subject is still a top driver of choice of major.

Read on for more findings and analysis of the survey, which asked about academics, health and wellness, involvement in campus life beyond the classroom, career readiness, and AI across the student experience.

Academics, Trust and AI

As in last year’s main Student Voice survey, most students approve of the education they’re getting so far, rating it as good (52 percent) or excellent (29 percent). This is relatively consistent across institution types. Nearly half of students (53 percent) report that they’re very well served by their institution’s course delivery options and schedules; that share increases, to 62 percent among respondents 25 and older and among community college students—those who may be in disproportionate need of extra flexibility. Most of the remainder indicate that they’re somewhat well served (37 percent over all).

Similarly, three in four students agree, somewhat (46 percent) or strongly (28 percent), that they trust their institution and believe it is reliable, cares about their well-being and acts with integrity—good news for a sector struggling to regain public confidence. Community college students are especially likely to strongly agree on trust, at 41 percent.

Closer to half of students over all agree that they trust colleges and universities in general (55 percent combined). Students are less trusting of their institution’s efforts to keep education affordable for students, however: Just 25 percent are very or extremely confident that their college or university is taking meaningful steps toward affordability, such as reducing unnecessary costs, limiting tuition increases or pooling resources—though this jumps to 44 percent among community college students. Twelve percent of students over all are highly confident that colleges and universities as a whole are taking meaningful steps to keep education affordable.

Looking more closely at the changing academic experience, eight in 10 students indicate that they use generative or agentic AI routinely. Asked about the biggest ways that AI is changing their approach to college, a third each say AI helps them complete coursework and study more efficiently and feel more confident understanding and tackling difficult concepts. Three in 10 say AI is making them less reliant on professors or tutoring centers for academic help. This can cut positively or negatively, since AI tools can make extra help more accessible while also potentially replacing valuable human interaction. More concretely on the negative side, 25 percent of all students report that they’ve changed how they write to avoid being falsely flagged by AI detectors, and 16 percent say they find themselves relying too heavily on AI to think or write on their own.

This is the full list of top ways generative or agentic AI has changed how students approach coursework, if at all; respondents could select up to three options:

They complete their coursework and study more efficiently: 34%

They feel more confident understanding and tackling difficult concepts: 33%

They rely less on professors or tutoring centers for academic help: 30%

They change how they write to avoid being falsely flagged by AI detectors: 25%

They do not use generative or agentic AI for college work: 20%

AI helps them be more organized or otherwise boosts accessibility: 19%

They find themself relying on AI too heavily to think or write on their own: 16%

AI has not changed how they approach college: 9%

For Tina R. Austin, an instructor and researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles, focused on AI literacy, metacognition and assessment redesign, the findings reflect what she sees in her own teaching: “Students are really more concerned than anyone else about their own learning,” she said. “They’re really distinguishing between AI just being there as a productivity tool and completing their work, and actually coming home and feeling like they learned something.”

Preserving learning in 2026 and beyond doesn’t mean abstaining from AI, she said, but rather purposely incorporating AI-free moments into the process. Austin has developed a teaching framework called UnBlooms, for example, that rethinks Benjamin Bloom’s taxonomy for an era in which machines can synthesize and generate. Ultimately, it seeks to help students become critical, appropriate users of AI and to help instructors grade students’ thinking, not just their output.

Austin said that faculty members are often introduced to AI tools in professional development settings that feel more like “tool talks,” emphasizing AI as a productivity booster instead of something that can advance their pedagogy. This can lead instructors to equate AI adoption with AI-augmented teaching, and students can lose motivation as a result, she said.

Students’ own definitions of responsible AI use in higher ed settings are similarly nuanced: Nearly two-thirds say it means helping them learn rather than simply doing work for them. Six in 10 say it’s about transparency in when and how AI is used. More than half each cite protecting students’ privacy, keeping humans involved in important decisions and giving students clear guidance on when and how to use AI.

A separate IHE/Hanover Research survey of 1,665 faculty members, published earlier this month, found that 88 percent said AI had somewhat or very negatively affected their confidence in the authenticity of students’ work or communications. Two in three said it had negatively affected trust between professors and students. But Student Voice respondents’ emphasis on transparency—coupled with other recent campus developments—suggest concerns about trust go both ways. At Eastern Illinois University, for instance, students this fall started a petition opposing professors’ use of AI as a “substitute” for learning materials. Supporters said they’re not trying to ban AI use, just to clarify its use as a tool, including through university policy. They want professors to disclose how and when they use AI in the classes. And they want the university to address the “root causes” of AI use, including growing faculty workloads.

Even with their nuanced views on AI, significant shares of Student Voice respondents think it has high or very high potential to improve the student experience in the following areas:

Academic help (e.g., supporting learning through AI-enabled tutors trained on the specific course material): 41%

Career planning (e.g., helping me build résumés, practice interviews and match skills to job openings): 33%

Student success coaching (e.g., giving personalized tips on time management, study habits and deadlines): 31%

Administrative services (e.g., speeding up campus tasks like housing applications, parking or tech support): 28%

Academic advising (e.g., giving instant guidance on major requirements and graduation tracking): 26%

Financial aid guidance (e.g., answering questions about my tuition bill, FAFSA and scholarships): 25%

Wellness support (e.g., connecting me quickly to campus mental health resources, stress-relief tools or coping strategies): 20%

Many student success administrators also see AI as having transformative potential for the student experience, according to the IHE/Hanover 2026 Survey of College and University Student Success Administrators—perhaps especially in light of their institutional capacity concerns.

Health and Well-Being

Even as AI reshapes academic life, students’ most frequently cited barriers to academic success are familiar: Mental health challenges top the list, with 41 percent citing stress, anxiety or depression that disrupts their focus or academic performance. This increases to 48 percent among respondents who have seriously considered stopping out of college. Financial pressure from insufficient financial aid or the need to work too many hours to cover living expenses follows, at 37 percent over all. This, too, increases to 48 percent for students who have thought about leaving college, underscoring the link between these two issues and persistence in the Student Voice data and in other research. Unengaging classes rank third over all, followed by difficulty staying connected or motivated. Other barriers, such as not seeing the purpose of college or navigating confusing campus systems, fall farther down the list. And even as financial pressures rank high, fewer—one in 10 students—cite a more chronic sense of basic needs insecurity, defined as struggling with stable housing, getting enough food or finding reliable transportation.

Just 11 percent of students over all say they do not experience significant barriers to academic success.

One more note: In this survey, 11 percent of students cite lack of academic preparation as a top barrier to student success. Among the student success administrators in their recent survey, 47 percent cited academic readiness as a top barrier.

Paralleling some of these findings, 28 percent of students rate their mental health as below average or poor. The same share say this of their financial well-being. Both are comparable to last year’s survey.

Sleep may be an underdiscussed struggle: 41 percent of students rate their sleep habits as below average or poor. About three in 10 give similarly low ratings to their nutrition and to their ability to manage stress. Students are somewhat more positive about their academic fit: 38 percent rate it above average or excellent, versus 31 percent for their sense of social belonging.

Just over a third (34 percent) rate their overall well-being as above average or excellent, while 51 percent say it’s average.

Financial strain is also apparent in the things students go without: More than six in 10 say they delayed or went without at least one essential in the past year for financial reasons. Thirty-one percent say they sacrificed sleep or rest because of paid-work obligations, and at least one in five each went without medical care, transportation, mental health care or food. Fifteen percent went without technology needed for school, and 14 percent went without medication. Consistent with the earlier finding on financial pressure versus more chronic basic needs insecurity, fewer indicate they’ve gone without housing or utilities.

For every category of need, students over 25 are more likely to report going without. Some 19 percent of students aged 18 to 24 have gone without food in the last year, for example, versus 30 percent of older students. Just a quarter of students 25 and up have not gone without any basic need, compared with 41 percent of their 18- to 24-year-old peers. And among students working 30 hours or more per week (n=915), just 21 percent haven’t gone without any essential for financial reasons in the last year.

Students also demonstrate limited awareness of emergency financial aid. Although three-quarters of student success administrators said in their survey that their institution offers some form of emergency aid, just 21 percent of Student Voice respondents say their college offers it. Sixty-two percent are unsure whether such aid exists. Only 13 percent say they know how to apply, and 7 percent say they have accessed it. This is similar to last year’s survey, and relatively consistent across respondents and institution types.

Jhenai Chandler, vice president for research, policy and student success at NASPA-Student Affairs Administrators in Higher Education, said her organization’s own top issues data reinforces the idea that student health, safety and well-being can’t rest with a single division or initiative. “Practitioners shared that while emergency aid programs and one-stop-shop models are essential,” she said of NASPA’s survey, “they often lack the capacity and resources to meet the scale of student need.” Supporting student success requires a “more comprehensive, institutionwide approach that integrates student well-being into institutional structures and is sustained through consistent funding and strong campus and community partnerships.”

Policy has an important role to play in helping establish sustainable funding sources, she added.

To the extent that AI can help connect students with resources, the National Student Legal Defense Network recently published guidelines for AI use in basic needs services, emphasizing privacy, accurate information, the continued centering of human staff and coordination with governments.

This year’s Student Voice survey also asked about online sports betting, prediction markets and other digital wagering. Fifteen percent of students say they have participated in such activities since enrolling, and 38 percent agree that digital wagering merits more attention at their institution. Few colleges and university are tracking digital wagering as a student success issue, however, according to IHE-surveyed administrators.

Additionally, relatively few students grasp the full cost of attendance, beyond tuition: 29 percent say they have a clear understanding of all costs, meaning there are no surprises and they can budget appropriately, similar to last year. This increases to 36 percent among students 25 and up. But more understanding of costs doesn’t necessarily equate to more financial security, since older students are also more likely to report unfulfilled basic needs.

Campus Connections

Despite these challenges, most students describe their campus’s climate positively: 73 percent say most or nearly all students at their institution feel welcomed, valued and supported. About a quarter say that only describes how some students feel. This is relatively consistent across the sample. Most students (76 percent) also say they feel somewhat or very supported in exploring different perspectives, even those that challenge their beliefs. In IHE’s 2026 Survey of College and University Chief Academic Officers with Hanover, 68 percent of provosts rated their campus’s overall climate for civil discourse as good or excellent.

The student survey also asked how recent federal actions seeking to limit college diversity, equity and inclusion efforts had affected the college experience, including respondents’ sense of belonging. Some 27 percent say those actions have negatively affected their experience, including 11 percent who describe the impact as significant. The share is higher among nonbinary students (68 percent negative, n=205) and Black students (35 percent, n=469), compared with 29 percent each of Hispanic (n=796) and Asian American and Pacific Islander students (n=808), and 24 percent of white students (n=2,490). Another 18 percent over all say they don’t feel personally affected but believe their peers have been negatively impacted. Nearly four in 10 (38 percent) report no real impact, while 11 percent say the impact has been positive to some degree.

Participation in campus life remains limited. Asked what would most encourage more campus involvement, if their institution could only invest in one approach, 40 percent over all and 42 percent of community college students endorse financial incentives such as compensation, stipends or tuition credits. (Student success leaders in their own survey tend to favor this approach as well, along with demonstrating the point of participation.)

Twenty percent of students favor more flexible opportunities that accommodate off-campus commitments, while 16 percent want dedicated, campuswide hours without scheduled classes and 14 percent say institutions should do a better job demonstrating the benefits of participation, such as direct career skills gained, networking opportunities or personal growth milestones. Nine percent endorse more virtual or hybrid options, increasing to 15 percent for students over 25.

As for how campus connections could help students falling through the cracks, these are the people students say they would turn to for support if they were struggling academically or personally, or considering leaving college, selecting all that apply:

Someone outside their institution (e.g., a family member or friend): 68%

A peer or fellow student: 46%

A specific academic adviser: 27%

A specific faculty member: 22%

A specific student support staff member (e.g., a counselor, coach or financial aid adviser): 21%

Another staff member they interact with regularly (e.g., a dining hall, custodial or security staff member): 9%

A specific administrator: 8%

No one: 5%

Not sure: 4%

Eleanor Eckerson Peters, senior director of research at the Institute for Higher Education Policy, said it makes sense that many students would turn to someone like a family member if they were struggling or thinking about leaving college. Yet the relatively small shares of students reporting that they would turn to faculty members, advisers or student support staff—and the 5 percent who say they would turn to no one—indicates that there’s “room for institutions to build stronger connections with their students,” she said. AI tools designed to encourage students to contact or connect with the right people and supports on campus—not replace human connection—hold promise here, she added, since nearly half of students already say they’d rely on a peer.

Preparing for What Comes Next

While outcomes matter more than ever, students’ views of postsecondary education’s value are not limited to earnings: Asked how college programs should be evaluated in light of new regulations tying program-level earnings outcomes to federal financial aid eligibility, 78 percent say programs should be judged primarily by the personal and educational value they provide, even if graduates do not earn higher salaries. Twenty-two percent favor judging programs primarily by their financial outcomes—a figure relatively consistent across the sample. Additionally, asked what informed their own choice of major once at college, 54 percent of students cite personal passion or interest in the field, ahead of factors such as expected salary and earning potential (34 percent), job-placement rates for graduates in the field (18 percent)—and even (and especially) the impact of AI and other technology on their career prospects (6 percent). About one in five cite flexibility for career changes (21 percent). This, too, is somewhat consistent across the sample.

Students’ access to information about postgraduate outcomes remains limited, however: 17 percent say they know detailed employment, salary or graduate school outcome data for their program, up from last year’s 12 percent. Some 46 percent know some general information. Just 14 percent say their college makes this information readily available; 11 percent are unsure where to find it.

Postcollege readiness is also a source of concern: Just 8 percent of respondents aren’t stressed in some way about preparing for life after college (one in five for those over 25), though their biggest sources of stress vary widely. From a long list of options, the largest share, 19 percent, cite worries about affording life after graduation. Some 16 percent cite overwhelming pressure to succeed, while 14 percent worry they don’t have enough internship or work experience.

What do students want their institutions to prioritize more to better prepare them for the job market? Like last year, direct connections between college and work rank highly: More than half want their college to expand job pipelines and internship opportunities.

This is what students say their institution should prioritize to better prepare them for the job market, selecting up to three options:

Job pipelines and internships: expanding company partnerships for internships, co-ops and hiring pipelines: 54%

Applied class projects: integrating more real-world projects and employer-aligned tasks directly into regular coursework: 35%

Résumé and interview training: better help with explaining their specific skills to employers and automated screening systems: 33%

Up-to-date coursework and credentials: updating class materials and credential options faster to match changing industry trends: 28%

Core career/durable skills: more focus on things like critical thinking, communication, ethics and teamwork in classes: 27%

Better career center resources: increasing staff, funding and specialized coaching at the campus career center: 22%

AI and digital literacy: more training on how to use emerging AI tools in their field: 11%

No changes needed: Their institution’s current career preparation is fully sufficient: 8%

Even with those wants, 80 percent of students somewhat or strongly agree that their college is preparing them with the skills, credentials and experiences they need to succeed in today’s job market.

Regarding the career-readiness trifecta of credential attainment, experiential readiness and skills articulation, student success administrators in their recent survey flagged relative student-readiness gaps in the latter two areas.

Amanda Butkiewicz, program director of Work + Learn at Arizona State University’s University College, said that higher ed needs to design the full student experience so that “meaningful work-based learning is built into students’ education, rather than dependent on their ability to seek out additional opportunities.” One way to do that? Embed industry-connected projects into coursework, which requires colleges to find ways for employers to engage beyond traditional internships and offer faculty the “autonomy, support and flexibility to integrate these experiences into their courses without unnecessary administrative barriers.”

Closing the skills-articulation gap also requires opportunities for reflection, Butkiewicz said, as leaders can’t just assume students recognize or can explain the skills they’re learning through campus employment, community engagement, leadership and coursework.

“Guided reflection should help students identify what they learned, how they applied it and what evidence demonstrates their growth,” she said. And pairing that reflection with a “tangible work product or portfolio artifact gives students something concrete to discuss and share.”

title: ‘Breakneck,’ China and Campus Construction Projects
summary:
‘Breakneck,’ China and Campus Construction Projects joshua.m.kim@d… Tue, 11/17/2026 - 03:00 AM A list of big university construction projects inspired by a fantastic book explaining why China is better at building big than the U.S. Byline(s) Joshua Kim ‘Breakneck,’ China and Campus Construction Projects
joshua.m.kim@d… Tue, 11/17/2026 - 03:00 AM

A list of big university construction projects inspired by a fantastic book explaining why China is better at building big than the U.S.

Byline(s)
Joshua Kim
full_text:
Breakneck: China’s Quest to Engineer the Future by Dan Wang

Published in August 2025

The core argument in Dan Wang’s superbly written and deeply reported book Breakneck is that China is run by engineers and an engineering mindset, whereas lawyers and legal thinking are dominant in the U.S. For Wang, who was born in China, grew up in Canada and the U.S., and has lived in China as an adult, this engineering-versus-legal framework is key to understanding both countries.

China’s political economy is built around national development and not the values of pluralism or the protection of individual rights. The ethos of prioritizing the good of the nation over the rights of the individual enables outstanding achievements such as China’s world-leading construction of high-speed rail (31,000 miles and counting). Other examples include the 118,500 miles of highways (compared to around 48,000 in the U.S.) and 560 miles of new metro lines in 2004 alone. Last year, China installed more new solar capacity than the rest of the world combined.

The price of all this national investment in infrastructure is that China has also brought an engineering mindset to social policy. The architect of the disastrous one-child policy, Song Jian, was not a demographer (thankfully) but an aerospace engineer. As Wang thoroughly documents in Breakneck, the average Chinese citizen pays a high price in terms of individual freedoms and access to a social safety net in exchange for the country’s ability to channel resources and override any opposition to large-scale infrastructure projects.

What makes Breakneck such a good book is the balance that Wang brings to his arguments. He wants the U.S. to be more like China in making long-term, large-scale investments (particularly in transportation, housing and clean energy) and for China to be more like the U.S. in its respect for individual rights and protections. Mostly, he wants those of us in the U.S. to be curious about how China has been able to leapfrog the U.S. in creating the conditions for world leadership in everything from electric vehicles to high-speed trains and clean energy.

Reading Breakneck, I kept thinking about how many of our college and university campuses have felt like giant construction zones over the past couple of decades. The U.S. can’t seem to build high-speed rail, but we have been good at building big on our college campuses. At the bottom of this review, I’ve included a list of the biggest campus building projects (nonmedical and nonstadium) that I’ve been able to find. (Let me know what I’m missing.)

One of the attributes I love about higher education is that, at our best, we combine a long-term, mission-driven strategic orientation with governance and funding structures that enable us to undertake big projects. The narrative about higher education is often negative. We seem to be constantly in crisis, with existential threats ranging from the demographic cliff to our susceptibility to cost disease to public disinvestment to the erosion of public faith in the value of a college degree.

Reading Breakneck is a reminder that the ability to make long-term investments in physical infrastructure, the place where China excels most, does not require a political structure as autocratic as China’s. Universities are not democracies, but we are pretty good (when compared to other types of organizations) at respecting individual autonomy and of promoting pluralistic beliefs. If you don’t think that is true, spend a minute working at a for-profit company and you will quickly come to realize that the typical person who works in higher ed has considerably more agency than the typical corporate employee.

Let’s get more curious on our campuses about both China and infrastructure.

What are you reading?

title: “Students are talking”: NUS president warns moving goalposts are costing Brand UK
summary:
International students are sharing their experiences of refusals and changing rules, and the UK's reputation is paying the price, warns Favour Samuel, the first international student to lead the National Union of Students (NUS) England.

The post “Students are talking”: NUS president warns moving goalposts are costing Brand UK appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
“Students are talking,” Samuel told parliamentarians, sector leaders and students gathered on November 17 at the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for International Students’ celebration of International Students Day.

“Every student who is overcharged, refused, or told the goalposts have moved goes and tells the next person… A country does not lose its reputation in one announcement; it loses it through one broken promise at a time,” she said.

Samuel described “a country that tells international students to come, takes their money, then changes the terms as they live life here in the UK. Rules that move after the payment has cleared… that is not how you welcome anyone”.

Samuel criticised the Home Office decision to ban study visas for Afghanistan, Sudan, Myanmar and Cameroon.

“There is a real fear that this list will continue growing, that Bangladesh, India, Ghana, Pakistan, and Nigeria could be next,” she said.

“If a passport can decide who deserves an education, then none of us are actually safe. When you treat people differently because of where they were born, you owe them a reason that is real, accurately tested, and proportionate.”

Samuel also raised concerns over a looming international student levy – which will see universities pay £925 per international student from 2028 to fund maintenance grants for domestic students – and noted that the government’s own analysis assumes some of the cost will be passed on to students.

“We want maintenance grants, but they cannot be tied to an unfair and unsustainable international student levy. You cannot fund one student support by taxing another.”

Earlier this month, the chancellor’s Budget outlined the move to restore the two-year Graduate Route only for graduates of some universities. For Samuel, this “does nothing but create a two-tier system”.

Conversations also centred on international students inclusion in net migration figures. Samuel said that “students need to be taken out of net migration figures”.

“We are sacrificing Britain’s international reputation and world-class universities to get down on arbitrary immigration figure… students need to be taken out of net migration figures,” said Samuel.

APPG co-founder Lord Karan Bilimoria, who came to the UK as an international student himself, has long called for students to be taken out of net migration figures. “It just doesn’t make sense,” he said. He pointed out that other countries count students when reporting to the UN but leave them out of their domestic figures.

Bilimoria set out the sector’s case in numbers, including a £42bn contribution to the economy and six local jobs supported by every 10 international students.

He also highlighted the role of international education in shaping global leadership, pointing to research showing that the UK continues to educate a significant proportion of the world’s leaders.

“You will be permanent ambassadors for British universities and for Britain, and a bridge between Britain and your countries and I welcome it,” he told international students gathered at the event.

The reception was the first in a series of events running over the next 12 months to mark the 10th anniversary of the APPG for International Students, which was founded in 2016.

The post When an Anatomy Practical Exam Becomes a Learning Event appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
In higher education, we often say we want students to move beyond memorization. Yet many of our exams still reward exactly that: recognize the correct answer, write it down, move to the next question.

In my own teaching, I began noticing a familiar pattern. Many students were doing well, but the lower-performing tail of the class seemed to be getting longer. These were not students who lacked potential. Many were working hard, but they were struggling to connect isolated facts into usable understanding.

That raised a simple question for me: Was my exam only measuring the gap, or could it help reduce it?

This question led me to redesign one practical exam using a format I now think of as collaborative reasoning with individual accountability. The goal was not to make the exam easier. The goal was to make students’ thinking more visible before they had to answer on their own.

The Problem With “Just Make it a Group Exam”

I did not want to simply turn the exam into a group test. That can create legitimate concerns: uneven participation, stronger students carrying weaker students, and students receiving credit for answers they may not understand.

At the same time, I did not want to ignore the value of peer discussion. Students often learn a great deal when they hear how classmates approach a problem, especially when the task requires reasoning rather than simple recall.

So the challenge became this: How do we let students benefit from discussion without removing individual accountability?

The solution was a two-phase exam station:

Group reasoning first

Individual answers second

Students could talk through the material, but every student still had to answer independently.

How the Format Worked

At each station, students first saw a set of tagged structures. Importantly, they did not see the questions yet.

They had a short period of time to discuss everything they knew about those structures. They could talk about identification, function, relationships, applications, or anything else that might matter.

Then the timer went off. Discussion stopped. Students flipped over the question card.

At that point, each student answered the questions individually. No talking. No group answer sheet. No shared score.

The format was simple:

Students examine the material.

Students discuss as a group.

Questions are revealed.

Students answer individually.

The group phase created the learning opportunity. The individual phase preserved accountability.

What Changed

When we compared student performance on a traditional exam with performance on the collaborative format, overall performance improved. But the more meaningful result was not the class average.

The biggest improvement came from students in the lower-performing quartiles.

That mattered to me. My goal was not to inflate grades across the board. My goal was to support the students who were struggling to make connections. The discussion seemed to give those students access to how their peers were reasoning before they had to retrieve and apply the information themselves.

The strongest students did not show the same level of improvement, likely because they were already performing near the top. But the lower tail moved, and that was the point.

What Students Thought

Student feedback was generally positive, especially around learning. Many students reported that discussion helped them understand the material more clearly and supported their individual answers.

But their feedback was not universally enthusiastic, and that is important.

Some students felt the individual answer period was too short. Others raised concerns about fairness and group dynamics. Some preferred the traditional format. Some preferred the collaborative format. Some had no strong preference.

That tension is useful. It tells us that the format has promise, but the details matter.

In future versions, I would keep the core structure but refine the timing. I would also be more explicit about expectations during the discussion phase:

Every student should contribute.

The goal is to explain reasoning, not just name answers.

Discussion should focus on relationships and applications.

Once the individual phase begins, all discussion stops.

This is not a shortcut. It is a structured thinking phase.

Why This May Work in Undergraduate Courses

Although I developed this format in an anatomy practical, the idea is not limited to anatomy or professional programs. It can work in many undergraduate courses where students need to apply concepts rather than simply recall facts.

In biology, students could examine a diagram, specimen, data figure, or microscopy image together before answering individual questions.

In chemistry, students could discuss a reaction mechanism, molecular structure, or lab scenario before individually predicting products or explaining errors.

In physics, students could reason through a diagram, graph, or conceptual problem before each student solves a related question independently.

In engineering, students could discuss a design constraint, system diagram, or failure scenario before individually explaining the next step.

In mathematics or statistics, students could discuss a problem setup, dataset, or model choice before independently completing a calculation or interpretation.

In humanities and social sciences, students could discuss a short passage, case, artifact, primary source, or policy scenario before writing an individual response.

The key is the sequence: Students discuss before seeing the questions. Then they answer individually.

That sequence matters. If students see the questions first, they may simply divide the work. If they discuss the material first, they must activate what they know more broadly. They prepare each other to think, not just to copy.

Why This Matters for Undergraduate Programs

Many undergraduate programs are concerned with persistence, DFW rates, first-generation student support, and performance gaps in gateway courses. Often, the students who struggle most are not unwilling to learn; they may simply lack access to the reasoning strategies that more experienced or confident students are already using.

This format gives them a brief window into those strategies.

They hear how peers identify key features, eliminate wrong ideas, connect concepts, and decide what matters. Then they must answer on their own.

That is the balance I find valuable: support without removing responsibility.

Practical Tips for Trying This Yourself

Faculty do not need to redesign an entire course to try this approach. Start small.

Use it for one quiz, one exam section, one lab practical, or a few problem-solving stations.

I would recommend:

Keep groups small: three to five students.

Hide the questions during the discussion phase.

Use a visible timer.

Keep individual answers short.

Use mostly foundational questions with a few deeper application questions.

Avoid group scores.

Collect feedback immediately afterward.

Tell students why you are using the format.

The last point matters. Students may assume group work means the exam will be easier. I tell them directly: this is not designed to make the exam easier. It is designed to make the thinking more visible.

Final Thought

Assessment does not have to be separate from learning. With careful design, it can become part of the learning process itself.

The lesson for me was not that every exam should become collaborative. They should not. The lesson was more practical: when students are allowed to reason together before answering individually, struggling students may get the support they need without removing accountability.

That is the kind of assessment worth building.

Dr. Pradeep Malreddy is a Clinical Associate Professor at Kansas State University, specializing in Anatomy and Histology. Holding a DVM from India and an MS from Kansas State, he brings a blend of clinical and academic expertise. He has additional certifications in Medical Education Research and Online Teaching from AAMC and Harvard. Dr. Malreddy has developed a One-Year Master’s Program at K-State and teaches courses in anatomy, histology, and physiology. His research focuses on anatomy education, eye-tracking technology, and active learning. An active member of professional organizations like the American Association of Veterinary Anatomists, he has received accolades for teaching excellence and diversity initiatives. He was recently honored with Fellowship in the United Kingdom’s prestigious Academy of Medical Educators.

title: Reaching Reserved Students in the Back Row: Strategies for Engagement

The post Reaching Reserved Students in the Back Row: Strategies for Engagement appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
The First Five Minutes: Traps and Snap Judgments

You walk into classroom 531 on the fifth floor, on a missive to deliver your best first lecture of the fall semester. You smile and say hello to your new students, expecting a wave of friendly faces in return. A few look up from their laptops and grin back, and you instantly decide these will be the “easy” students who like you best. You like them best, too. You take your place at the podium when a student texting on their phone catches your eye. A sudden thought flits across your mind: this student may be trouble. Just like that, assumptions are formed before class even begins. First impressions can stick.

From an evolutionary standpoint, this urge to make snap judgments makes you more than just judgy. It is an adaptive survival mechanism rather than a superficial flaw (Zebrowitz, 2017). Our human ancestors had to rapidly assess the lay of the land to detect threats, so gut reactions kept them safe. But in a modern college classroom free from creatures and carnivores, that ancient instinct can lead to a severe misassessment of the terrain. When a student meets your greeting with silence or a blank stare, their quiet response most likely has nothing to do with you.

Deciphering the Blank Stare

A flat expression is not an automatic sign of hostility, an indictment of your teaching, or a sign of personal animosity. In reality, a reserved student is usually dealing with one of a dozen unspoken realities. The quiet one in the back might be a first-generation student who has never stepped foot inside a college classroom. Another might be experiencing imposter syndrome, afraid to stand out. Some students simply land lower on the extroversion or openness scales, while others may be dealing with physical or mental health challenges that make emotional expressions more difficult to muster. It could simply be that they are daydreaming, having a difficult day, or lost in a laptop screen.

While managing screens is a real challenge—one that can be addressed by keeping a room mostly tech-free and offering old-school notebooks and pens as incentives as I do—the main takeaway is simple. An inexpressive or stoic student is not an adversary. But it makes sense why your brain may register them as one. When someone gives you a still face, you instinctively flag the expression as a threat to the relationship. Because humans are meaning-makers, we interpret a blank face as rejection. Inattention and disengagement may be just as damaging as actual conflict because it leaves you stuck in an uncertain state, wondering if you matter to the other person (Tronick, 1989).

The Neural Overlap of Rejection

This connection between social rejection and physical pain is deeply biological. Research from a meta-analysis of over 500 published studies shows that when rejection is powerfully elicited, like having someone who recently experienced an unwanted breakup view a photograph of their ex-partner, the specific brain regions that support the sensory components of physical pain, such as the secondary somatosensory cortex and the dorsal posterior insula, become highly active (Kross et al., 2011).

This means that social heartbreak and physical injury share the same neural real estate. When brain scans look at someone experiencing severe rejection, the areas lighting up are the same ones that register an actual physical injury, like a broken bone or a burn. Your brain does not distinguish between a wounded body and a wounded ego. These results give literal meaning to the idea that rejection hurts! It is no surprise that our language equates social pain and estrangement with words typically reserved for physical injury, like being crushed, shattered, or having a broken heart (Eisenberger & Lieberman, 2004).

From Cooing to Crying: The Psychology of the Blank Face

It is human nature to like people who like us. We tend to withdraw from those who shun us with a still face. This phenomenon traces back to Edward Tronick’s famous psychology experiment, which demonstrated how a mother’s neutral, still face left a baby feeling sequestered and scared.

To visualize this, picture a mother and her baby interacting, facing each other, smiling, and playing. Everything feels warm and connected. Suddenly, the mother goes completely blank. No smile, no reaction, just a neutral, stony expression, like her face just went on pause. At first, the baby tries to get her attention by smiling, cooing, and waving their little arms. When that fails, confusion turns to frustration. Some babies cry or scream before eventually collapsing into a state of helpless withdrawal. From their perspective, the safe emotional connection is gone, and they cannot get it back (Tronick et al., 1978).

The Trap of the Negative Narrative

Babies are hardwired to demand social reciprocity, but professors enjoy no such evolutionary leverage. While it’s hard not to react negatively to a face that seems unwelcoming,

We cannot throw a tantrum, scream, or shake our fists in the air to force a student to pay attention, smile back at us, or put their phone away. Likewise, publicly singling out a seemingly disengaged student with a sarcastic or critical remark is never effective. This can easily fracture the classroom climate and make everyone feel uncomfortable. A successful classroom fosters group cohesion, creating the emotional bond and sense of belonging that transforms a room of individuals into a supportive learning community (Yalom & Leszcz, 2020). Without that foundational safety, trust can evaporate and tension can spread.

I teach in the psychology department, so I’d like to think that my background has helped me foster a more patient, caring perspective toward students. When I walk into a classroom and cheerfully ask, “How was your break?” and am met with indifference by a few students, I am aware of the importance of avoiding snap judgements or viewing the class as an amorphous whole. Teachers who assume a class is distant or chilly will naturally start to pull back to protect their own warmth.

Attachment Styles in the Classroom

Instead of worrying about rejection, instructors can zoom out and recognize that “still faces” may reflect a student’s childhood attachment style. Avoidant and anxious individuals tend to maintain the same behavioral patterns in school as they do in their interpersonal relationships, using attachment as an innate emotion regulation system to modulate stress (Fraley & Roisman, 2019).

When we view the classroom through this lens, we can cautiously seek out the students who may never otherwise visit our office hours. According to research by Gore and Rogers (2010), a student’s childhood attachment style significantly influences how they handle academic goals. Their study found that securely attached students tend to thrive and earn higher grades when their academic motivations are tied to the interests of important people in their lives. In other words, when a secure student knows their parents are proud of them, or when they have a professor who checks in on them, it acts like fuel. They think, “People care about me and want me to succeed,” and that makes them study harder and get better grades.

In contrast, avoidant students may eschew the involvement of others. Even when a professor reaches out with genuine support, offers help, or tries to learn about their goals, an avoidant student may panic. To them, your involvement feels like pressure, control, or a trap (Gore & Rogers, 2010). From the theoretical perspective of Rentzios and Karagiannopoulou (2021), this behavior is an intentional, self-protective strategy used to regulate overwhelming emotions during the learning process. Because avoidant students may view closeness with an authority figure (the professor) as dangerous or unstable, they might keep that bonding instinct firmly turned off, projecting a lack of interest.

In this way, a student’s blank gaze, apparent boredom, or surface-level effort is actually a sophisticated psychological defense mechanism (Rentzios & Karagiannopoulou, 2021). It is a behavioral pattern meant to avoid emotional risk by keeping both the course material and the professor at a safe, non-threatening distance.

Making Space in Room 531

In my classroom, I’m not trying to force an introverted or anxious student to become a bubbly extrovert. I’m just trying to show them that I am a reliable, safe professional. When an avoidant student realizes that their still face doesn’t make me upset, lose energy, or pull back my support, their defense system often slowly begins to deactivate.

I believe the worst thing a teacher can do is give up on a quiet, reserved class by delivering a cold or distant lecture. Instead, we must show up with the same level of enthusiasm, structure, warmth, and clarity every single week. Ultimately, a blank face is not a personal insult or a threat to our authority. Once we drop defensiveness or snap judgments, we create space for genuine connection, setting the stage for a positive classroom culture that supports learning and growth.

Dr. Wertheimer is a child and adolescent psychotherapist, certified life coach, and author specializing in pedagogy and mental health. A Vision for Modernized Learning

“Schools need to deliver flexible spaces for learning everywhere,” Ortiz says, and that can be difficult to do when IT teams are managing a vast array of fragmented legacy solutions. To deliver seamless learning, “we all need to strive for really simple and consistent experiences that require little or no training.”

Smart video enablement and broader digitalization offer a way forward. The right audiovisual elements, intelligent cameras, classroom control systems, lecture capture and collaboration platforms answer the call, especially when paired with a thoughtful approach to implementation.

Modernization needs to be a collaborative process, with faculty, students and IT all exploring the needs and identifying the right approaches.

“I don’t think these solutions can be designed in a vacuum,” Ortiz says. “When people are part of the process and the decision-making, then they believe in it. You have their buy-in.”

Click the banner below for the tools to support today’s classrooms.

As that shared vision emerges, there are products that can help deliver on the promise of modernization in support of seamless learning experiences across all environments.

How Modern Classroom Technology Helps Enable Learning Anywhere

Every college and university will have unique needs, but some common elements are worth looking at.

Many schools have pivoted to hybrid classes. To support those institutions’ needs, “Logitech has a full array of videoconferencing cameras that are purpose-built for education,” Ortiz says.

For example, Scribe is an AI whiteboard camera with a custom lens for videoconferencing. Reach is an adjustable content camera for sharing nondigital content. With these tools in play, “it is much easier for a professor to share content with students,” she says.

The Rally AI Camera Pro offers AI-based RightSight 2 technology, which intuitively frames every active participant or a professor giving a lecture.

“Suppose, for example, I’m giving a lecture and moving around the room. With Presenter View, advanced intelligence keeps presenters perfectly in frame, so instructors can deliver with ease while remote viewers stay connected and engaged, every step of the way,” Ortiz says.

READ MORE: AV over IP technology makes classrooms easier to manage.

All teachers need solutions that are easy to manage. “They want to avoid lost time at the start of class,” Ortiz says. That means, “you want consistency between rooms, and you want that training burden to go away.”

To that end, Logitech offers a Logitech Tap, a touch-screen controller that offers one-touch join calendar integration for quick videoconferencing, and instant content sharing that makes it easy for a professor to launch a collaborative learning experience. And there are personal workspace solutions as well, aimed at supporting teachers’ productivity.

That includes the right keyboards and mice, as well as solutions like Spotlight 2, an advanced presentation remote with haptic feedback. Receive instant confirmation that you've pressed the highlight button through subtle haptic vibrations. You can zoom in on a particular area of content and can customize that view, “allowing for different highlighting effects,” Ortiz says.

Spotlight 2 even helps people who get nervous when presenting. “It times you for breathing exercises, and it vibrates to guide you: ‘Okay, breathe now,’” she says. That haptic capability helps the lecturer remain focused and makes for a better student experience.

REVIEW: The Logitech Spotlight 2 keeps presenters focused.

All these tools are delivered in a way that simplifies the work for the IT teams tasked with delivering technology in support of seamless learning. “We pride ourselves on offering solutions that are not only easy to use but also easy to support and scale,” Ortiz says.

She points to Sync, a videoconferencing device management software product that helps everyone stay connected by ensuring their Logitech video collaboration devices are healthy and up to date. “IT teams, especially those supporting a huge campus, can use our device management solutions to remotely troubleshoot or update all the units directly from their desk,” she says.

“Sync also supports a meeting room dashboard. A consolidated view of room status and device inventory gives IT valuable insight into every flex desk and video meeting room, and they can provide better support and make decisions about resources moving forward,” she says.

In today’s competitive era in higher ed, a positive learning experience matters. With the right technology supporting in-person, hybrid, HyFlex and fully remote learning, “schools can provide a much better learning experience overall,” Ortiz says. “They can deliver consistent, high-quality instruction, with a model that is repeatable across all learning spaces.”
